Summary:
Quick retrospective on week 2 of the Straightline pilot. Focus: continuous batching behavior, concurrency targets, queueing jitter observed during 10-12x burst, and action items to validate steady-state economics.

Topics:
1) Observed throughput profile and p50/p95 latency drift
2) KV cache warm vs cold effects
3) Concurrency ceiling and safe fallback policy
4) Playbook for production ramp and Dedicated conversation

Transcript body:
[00:00] Elliot (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Jordan, Priya, Sam, you all good?
[00:04] Jordan (Straightline): Yeah, all good. Quick note, we pulled in the new patch you sent this morning, Maya, thanks.
[00:09] Maya (Redwood SE): cool cool, so this call is mostly to review the throughput runs from last night and tune the concurrency targets. I pulled the traces, there was a chunk between 01:12 and 01:45 UTC that looks like queue depth spiking then backpressure kicked in.
[00:23] Priya (Straightline): yep, we saw about a 12% drop in successful requests during that window, p95 latency jumped to ~1.8s, p50 to 280ms. We narrowed it to a combination of cold kv cache on a subset of requests and a burst of large inputs.
[00:40] Maya: right, the model's KV cache warmup cost is disproportionately affecting the first 3-4 tokens for those big contexts. We documented the kv-cache warm strategy in the README but real traffic is messier, of course. (laugh)
[00:52] Sam (CTO): question — is that KV cache thing something we can pre-warm per route, or are we looking at always-on Dedicated to avoid that penalty?
[00:59] Elliot: good question. You can pre-warm with a prefix cache technique or keep a small pool pinned on Dedicated. The tradeoff is cost vs. the latency SLO. For your 99% latency target at 300ms, Dedicated with pinned instances helps but you pay for that reservation.
[01:18] Jordan: we are targeting a p95 of <600ms for customer-facing inference, and can tolerate 2-3x higher for async batch pipelines. So maybe 600ms p95 is our hard goal for sync.
[01:27] Maya: given that, we recommended a concurrency envelope of 8-12 for the current model and instance type. In the night run we tested 6, 8, 12, and 16. At 16 we saw continuous batching kick in and larger batches which reduced per-token cost but the queueing jitter spiked.
[01:46] Priya: that’s the issue — throughput looked great at 16 but some requests got stuck behind long-running large-context calls and the local queue grew past the 500ms threshold.
[01:56] Maya: we think a safer default is 10 concurrent worker threads plus the continuous-batching cap to ~48 tokens per batch at your median payload. That keeps tail latency from regressing while preserving batching efficiency.
[02:12] Jordan: can you explain the continuous batching cap again? I got the basic idea but the numbers matter.
[02:17] Maya: sure. Continuous batching groups inflight requests onto the same decode step until either a max batch size or a time window elapses. The cap ensures a single request doesn't allow the batch to grow unbounded — for example, if you have a very long context it won't block 20 short requests from moving through. So we set a per-request contribution limit (like max 12 tokens per request to the batch) and a batch token cap (~48 tokens). That gave us good tradeoffs in sim.
[02:50] Sam: do we need custom kernel/quantization changes? We noticed the cost numbers at 12 concurrency still looked higher than expected compared to your public benchmarks.
[02:58] Elliot: two things — first, the public benchmarks are median-case with warm cache and homogenous inputs. Real traffic variance matters. Second, quantization and kernel selection on your specific model variant are slightly different; our runtime switched to an alternate kernel at high-seq lengths which increased latency a hair in that run. Maya can point to the exact step.
[03:16] Maya: yeah, on our trace the runtime selected the fallback kernel at sequence >1024 for about 7% of tokens. That is fixable by forcing a different kernel choice or nudging the batch cap down. We added a kernel-selection flag in the patch.
[03:30] Priya: ok, from operations POV, what's the easiest short-term change we can apply to reduce the p95 spikes?
[03:35] Maya: short-term: enable aggressive kv-cache prefixing for your 3 highest-volume routes, reduce concurrency from 16 -> 10, and set continuous-batching caps to 48 tokens and per-request token contribution to 12. Long-term: run a steady-state Dedicated test to see tail improvements.
[03:52] Jordan: sounds reasonable. Any concerns about throughput drop? We care about tokens/sec for billing.
[03:57] Elliot: expect a small drop in peak tokens/sec — maybe 8-12% vs the 16 concurrency run — but unit-cost per token may still improve because fewer timeouts and retries. We will provide a token-level cost chart.
[04:12] Priya: we'll run the 2-hr with those settings tonight and upload logs. Is there anything special to turn on for tracing?
[04:18] Maya: include debug-level trace for 00:00-02:00 UTC and enable token-level sampling on routes. We can correlate traces to queue depth buckets.
[04:28] Sam: one more question: if we eventually move to Dedicated, how quickly can you provision a small pinned pool?
[04:34] Elliot: typical lead time is a week for a reserved pool in a new tenancy, faster in the same region. We can also use short-term burst capacity in the hosted plane while you validate.
[04:44] Jordan: competitor angle: we evaluated Vertex AI's inference endpoints briefly; they have auto-scaling but less built-in KV cache awareness. Do you see that in your other customers?
[04:53] Maya: yes, competitors often rely on simple autopilot, but they don't have request-level KV caching and continuous-batching heuristics tuned for LLM workflows. That’s one of our differentiators.
[05:04] Priya: note: in the last run we also saw a handful of 429s originating from our orchestration layer when the pod readiness probe lagged during a kube rollout — not Redwood's runtime. We flagged that separately.
[05:15] Elliot: good catch. Keep orchestration traces. For this call recap, we should list explicit next steps.
[05:22] Maya: agreed. I'll also assemble a one-page playbook for backpressure handling — how to trim queues, recommended circuit breaker thresholds, and how to set the continuous-batching caps.
[05:30] Sam: ok, that helps. Jordan, Priya, anything else?
[05:33] Jordan: no, just want the cost chart and the playbook.
[05:36] Priya: we want the 2hr run artifacts by Monday so we can decide Dedicated vs hosted for tier-1.
[05:42] Elliot: we'll target that.

Recap (verbatim):
- Short-term tuning: concurrency -> 10, batch token cap -> 48, per-request contribution -> 12, enable kv-cache prefixing for top routes.
- Run: Straightline to execute 2-hr steady-state with KV warm and mixed payloads (Priya).
- Artifacts: Elliot to share cost chart and tuned config, Maya to deliver backpressure/playbook.
- Follow-up: schedule a Dedicated provisioning discussion week of 2027-09-27 if metrics justify.
